metric_rationale: Trial 1 provides the strongest possible dissociation between the two theories. Option A wins on two high-validity features, while Option B wins on three lower-validity features. Tallying simply counts the features and prefers B (3 vs 2), whereas WADD weighs them by validity and prefers A (1.85 vs 1.65). By measuring the proportion of times Option A is chosen on this specific trial, we obtain a metric that is near 0 for Tallying and near 1 for WADD.

The metric isolates the two trial types where WADD and Tallying have completely opposite strict preferences. In Trial 1 (A=[1,1,0,0,0] vs B=[0,0,1,1,1]), WADD prefers A due to high-validity features, while Tallying prefers B due to a higher total count of features. In Trial 2, the options are swapped. We calculate the difference in the probability of choosing B in Trial 2 versus Trial 1. WADD will strongly tend towards +1, whereas Tallying will strongly tend towards -1.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. TTB processes features lexicographically according to their validity, meaning it always chooses the option favored by the most valid discriminating cue. WADD, on the other hand, integrates all cues and can frequently choose the opposite option on 'compensatory' trials (e.g., when the single best cue favors Option A, but multiple weaker cues favor Option B). By measuring the exact adherence to TTB's deterministic predictions, we can strongly discriminate between the two models: data generated by TTB will score highly on this metric (modulo noise), while data generated by WADD will score significantly lower due to its compensatory nature.

In the provided experimental design, the trials are structured such that when option B has more positive features than option A, option A nevertheless possesses the single most valid cue. Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose option A (response 0) because it stops searching at the first discriminating cue. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all cues, allowing the coalition of multiple lower-validity cues in option B to outweigh the single high-validity cue in option A, leading to a higher rate of choosing option B (response 1). Thus, the proportion of B choices on these specific trials will be substantially higher under WADD compared to TTB.

This metric calculates the difference in the rate of TTB-consistent choices between 'Agreement' trials (where TTB and WADD favor the same option) and 'Conflict' trials (where they favor opposing options). Because pure TTB's decision mechanism yields identical choice probabilities across all trials (its score vector is always [1, 0] or [0, 1]), its expected value for this difference is exactly 0. In contrast, the Strategy Mixture theory allows WADD to pull choices away from the TTB winner on conflict trials, making the TTB-consistency rate significantly lower on conflict trials than on agreement trials. Consequently, this difference will be strongly positive for Mixture and zero for pure TTB, providing a highly robust discriminator.

This metric isolates 'compensatory conflict' trials where the pure Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic strongly predicts choosing Option A (because the most valid discriminating cue favors A), while the Weighted Additive (WADD) component strongly favors Option B (because a coalition of lower-validity cues outvotes the single best cue). The pure TTB model will rarely choose B on these trials (only due to general noise), whereas the Strategy Mixture model will choose B significantly more often due to the compensatory influence of the WADD component. By computing the proportion of B choices specifically on these conflict trials, we obtain a sensitive measure that discriminates the two theories.

This metric measures the sensitivity of choices to the third cue in trials where the first two cues strongly agree. In trials 3 and 4 (and symmetrically 7 and 8), the first two cues point in the same direction. For Threshold-based Sequential Search (TSS), the cumulative evidence after the first two cues is 1.7, which strictly exceeds the maximum possible threshold (1.25). Thus, TSS will always stop searching early and ignore the third cue, resulting in a choice difference of zero between these trials. In contrast, the Strategy Mixture evaluates all cues via its WADD component. The third cue shifts the WADD evidence by 1.4, which systematically alters the choice probabilities. Consequently, this metric will be approximately 0 for TSS, but significantly greater than 0 for the Mixture model.

This metric compares the rate at which subjects choose the Take-The-Best (TTB) favored option when TTB and WADD agree (Trial 6) versus when they conflict but the first two cues point in the same direction (Trials 1 and 4). For the Threshold-based Sequential Search (TSS) model, the accumulated evidence after the first two cues in Trials 1 and 4 is 1.75, which exceeds the maximum possible threshold (1.25). Thus, TSS terminates early and chooses the TTB option on Trials 1/4 just as reliably as it does on Trial 6, yielding a difference near 0 (with very low between-subject variance). In contrast, the Strategy Mixture model evaluates TTB and WADD independently. On Trial 6, both models agree, so the TTB option is chosen ~100% of the time. On Trials 1 and 4, TTB and WADD conflict, so the TTB option is only chosen according to the mixture probability. This results in a large, positive difference (~0.5 on average) for the Strategy Mixture model, robustly discriminating the two theories.

In Trial 1 (A=[1,0,0,0,0], B=[0,1,1,1,1]) and Trial 4 (A=[1,0,1,0,0], B=[0,1,0,1,1]), the first cue strongly favors A (evidence +0.9). In Threshold-based Sequential Search (TSS), if the threshold is <= 0.9, search stops immediately at cue 1 and A is chosen for BOTH trials. If the threshold > 0.9, search continues. In both trials, the maximum cumulative evidence never exceeds 0.9 again, so TSS searches to the end. At the end, both trials have negative cumulative evidence for A (-1.7 for Trial 1, -0.3 for Trial 4), so B is chosen. Thus, TSS predicts identical choice probabilities for Trial 1 and Trial 4 (P(A) difference is ~0). In contrast, Probabilistic Stopping Sequential Search (PSSS) is sensitive to the intermediate evidence. Trial 4 has much stronger intermediate evidence for A (+0.8 at step 3) compared to Trial 1 (-0.6 at step 3), leading to a higher probability of stopping and choosing A. Thus, PSSS predicts P(A | Trial 4) > P(A | Trial 1).

We partition 11 of the 14 trials into 'Strong' trials (where the first two cues agree) and 'Weak' trials (where the first two cues disagree). In all 11 of these trials, Threshold-based Sequential Search (TSS) predicts that the option favored by the first cue will ALWAYS be chosen, regardless of the subject's threshold. This is because the accumulated evidence either triggers an early stop favoring the first cue, or the search proceeds to the end where the final tally still favors the first cue. Consequently, TSS predicts identical choice probabilities for the Cue 1 winner across both groups (expected difference = 0). In contrast, Probabilistic Stopping Sequential Search (PSSS) evaluates evidence continuously. In Strong trials, evidence rapidly accumulates to high magnitudes (+/- 1.7 by step 2), leading to early stopping with high confidence. In Weak trials, evidence drops to near zero at step 2, prolonging search and exposing the decision to intermediate reversals (where PSSS might stop and choose the wrong option) or ending with much weaker final evidence. Thus, PSSS predicts a significantly lower probability of choosing the Cue 1 winner in Weak trials compared to Strong trials, yielding a strong positive difference that cleanly discriminates the theories while utilizing a large pool of trials to minimize empirical variance.
